newsitem.title: CHINA: Japan minister seeks better ties in China talks.
newsitem.headline: Japan minister seeks better ties in China talks.

text.p: Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda and top Chinese leaders on Sunday agreed to follow Tokyo's symbolic resumption of grant aid to Beijing with efforts to further mend the battered Sino-Japanese relationship.

Japanese officials said both sides agreed in principle to an exchange of visits this year by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and Chinese Premier Li Peng, with Chinese President Jiang Zemin expected to travel to Tokyo in 1998.
Ikeda met Jiang and Li on Sunday, one day after signing an agreement that lifted a ban on grant aid imposed by Tokyo in protest at Chinese nuclear weapons testing.

Both Ikeda and Jiang had signalled their willingness to work hard for better relations during 1997, the 25th anniversary year of the establishment of diplomatic relations between Tokyo and Beijing, said Foreign Ministry spokesman Hidehiko Hamada.
"The foreign minister... expressed his wish to further improve bilateral relations between Japan and China in this commemorative year," Hamada told a news briefing.

Japanese officials say ties with Beijing have warmed greatly since being chilled last year by disputes over a contested island group in the East China Sea and by Hashimoto's visit to a controversial Tokyo war shrine.

The disputes, along with friction over Chinese nuclear weapons testing, a Japan-U.S. security pact and the legacy of Tokyo's imperial past, had helped drive relations to what Japanese officials called their lowest ebb since 1972.
Ikeda had told Li it was normal for any 25-year marriage to experience problems, and that such disputes were the inevitable result of the intimacy of matrimony, Hamada said.
"Once (we) got married, suddenly we have to live together... of course, (we) may find some problems -- because the basic relations are much closer," he said.
Ikeda had on Saturday moved to boost relations with China when he said Japan would consider dropping its co-sponsorship of a United Nations motion critical of Beijing's human rights record.

In a meeting with his Chinese counterpart Qian Qichen, the Japanese foreign minister also signed a note for a 1.7 billion yen ($13.7 million) grant for a medical aid project in China's eastern city of Nanjing.

The formal agreement to resume grant aid brought an end to Tokyo's mostly symbolic freeze on about 7.0 billion yen of aid a year that was implemented in August 1995 to protest a Chinese nuclear weapons test.
Beijing announced an indefinite moratorium on testing last year.
Ikeda's visit, the first by a Japanese foreign minister since 1995, was scheduled to end on Sunday.

Japanese officials said the foreign minister had refused to give ground on one of the key irritants in relations last year by repeating Tokyo's claims to a group of East China Sea islands known in Chinese as the Diaoyus and in Japanese as the Senkakus.
Tokyo had legal claim to the islands and rejected Beijing's view that they were part of Chinese territory -- but did not want to see the issue further harm relations, Hamada said.

Japanese officials have said Ikeda's visit aimed to steer clear of major Sino-U.S. problem issues in order to focus on more fruitful areas for cooperation, and Hamada said neither side had raised the issue of Senkakus sovereignty.
While sovereignty issues took a back seat, the foreign minister had told Beijing it needed to do more to gain entry to the World Trade Organisation, they said.
He had also tried to reassure Beijing that the Japan-U.S. security alliance was not aimed against it, they said but gave no details.
